speaker: SPEAKER_01
transcript: Today, I'm thrilled to share a new conversation I recently had with the Congresswoman about this historic moment and other timely topics, but first, a bit more about her. Barbara Lee has served in Congress for over 25 years. Lee first got involved in politics when she met Shirley Chisholm and worked on Chisholm's presidential campaign in 1972. Chisholm made history as the first black woman in Congress and as the first black woman to seek a presidential nomination from a major political party. Now, with Kamala Harris as our first Black and South Asian woman on the ballot for president, Lee reflects on what Chisholm might think of where we are today and shares her own thoughts on this current political moment. As the first Black woman elected to the State Senate from Northern California and the highest-ranking Black woman appointed to Democratic leadership, Lee has been a trailblazer who has always been a strong advocate for increasing Black women's representation in politics. She is also known for being an outspoken proponent of peace, advancing legislation to address HIV and AIDS and end poverty. Lee coined the phrase War on Women when Republican lawmakers were pushing to strip critical funding for women's health care services. Earlier this year, Lee stepped up to run for the Senate seat vacated after Senator Dianne Feinstein's passing. Although Lee was defeated in the Senate primary and will leave Congress in January, she insists she's, quote, not retiring and will keep working from the outside to, quote, get a lot done. In this insightful interview, the Congresswoman and I discuss what it would mean if Harris is elected as our first woman and women of color president, what's at stake in this coming election and what her call to action is. Why having black women's perspectives and leadership is so important? What we can do to get more women in diversity into politics? What's next for her and more? It is so wonderful to speak to you again. You were always one of my favorite people to talk to. And of course, reflecting back to when I interviewed you all those years ago for my book, What Will It Take to Make a Woman President? A momentous time for us to be talking again. So just to sort of even start there, we are in a historic moment where the U.S. could potentially elect Kamala Harris as our first black and South Asian woman president. What would it mean to young boys and girls in this country and to women's leadership generally to finally break the glass ceiling and elect a woman president who is also a woman of color? And what does it personally mean to you?
